question: Which market structure gives MOST pricing power?
before: Monopolist = sole seller, no direct competition, maximum price-setting ability. Perfect competition = zero (price-taker). Monopolistic = some via differentiation. Oligopoly = significant but constrained by rivals.
after:
Concept: Pricing power is the ability of a firm to set prices above marginal cost without losing all customers to competitors. It depends directly on the number of competitors and availability of substitutes in a market.

Why this is correct: A monopoly is the only market structure where a single firm is the sole seller with no close substitutes. Because customers have no alternatives, the monopolist can raise prices substantially without losing demand to rivals, giving it maximum pricing power.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Perfect competition: Firms are price-takers, not price-makers. With many identical sellers and perfect information, any firm raising price above market rate loses all customers instantly. Pricing power is zero.

B) Monopolistic competition: Firms have some pricing power through product differentiation (brand, quality, location), but this is limited. Many competitors exist, so customers can switch to substitutes if prices rise too much. Pricing power is weak.

C) Oligopoly: A few large firms have significant pricing power, but it is constrained by mutual interdependence. Each firm must consider rivals' reactions to price changes. Pricing power is moderate, not maximum.

Intuition: In equity research, identifying a company's market structure is critical to valuing its competitive moat and margin sustainability. A true monopoly or near-monopoly (e.g., a utility with regulatory protection) can maintain high margins and raise prices with minimal volume loss, making it highly attractive to investors. Perfect competitors, by contrast, are commodity producers with razor-thin margins and no pricing flexibility.
